newsitem.title: CROATIA: Bosnian, Croatian leaders to meet in Split.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian, Croatian leaders to meet in Split.

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and Bosnia's presidency chairman Alija Izetbegovic will meet on Wednesday in the Adriatic port of Split to discuss the Bosnian peace agreement, under the scrutiny of American envoys.
The summit has been delayed several times and will now take place as international pressure on all the former warring factions in Bosnia is intensifying.

U.S. diplomat Richard Holbrooke will time his return to the Balkans to coincide with the summit where he is due to meet both leaders. He is coming to pressure all parties into faster implementation of the peace accord he engineered in Dayton, Ohio in 1995 and will also visit Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic while in the region.
The meeting will provide Tudjman with his first opportunity to put into practice promises he made at his inauguration in Zagreb on Tuesday.
"We pledge our support to Dayton (peace accord) and the Federation," he told a gathering of the highest state, army and church officials and foreign ambassadors.

Yet his support for several aspects of Dayton has been found wanting. The United States has led criticism of him for failing to use his influence over his Bosnian Croat proteges who have refused to hand over suspected war criminals and have often undermined the Moslem-Croat Federation which makes up half of post-war Bosnia.
Moslems and Croats allied in the federation in 1994 which was brokered under U.S. diplomacy.

Tudjman also said at the ceremony: "I solemnly declare that I shall be an impartial president of all Croats and Croatian citizens, regardless of their political and other affiliations," implying he considers Croats in other countries as his subjects. Many of them view him as their president.

Bosnian Croats living across the border from Croatia see themselves as Croatian citizens -- they vote in Croatian elections, their car licence plates are indistinguishable from Croatian plates and they use the Croatian flag and currency.
Izetbegovic, the Moslem chairman of the presidency, and Tudjman have had stormy relations ever since the two men led their republics to break away from the old Yugoslav federation.
Tudjman was anxious to hold the meeting earlier to prove to the United States and European governments that he was lending his support to the troubled federation.

But Izetbegovic had declined to meet Tudjman for months until Zagreb made good on previous commitments. After coming under heavy Western pressure, Tudjman pushed the Bosnian Croats in the southern town of Mostar into agreeing a unified police force last month.
Croat-controlled towns in central Bosnia have also begun allowing the return of Moslem refugees who were expelled during a 10-month Moslem-Croat war in 1993.

Over the weekend hundreds of Moslem refugees who had recently moved back to their pre-war homes around the Croat-controlled town of Jajce were forced to flee under intimidation and threats from angry, drunken Croat mobs.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Tuesday he expected Tudjman to condemn the events in Jajce, and was clearly hoping he would do so at Wednesday's summit.
Tudjman is still seen to have enormous influence over the Bosnian Croat community. Zagreb had no comment about the weekend incidents.
